view: The construction with 'when' makes the owners' answer follow their seeing the garden immediately and instinctively.
The owners' awakening from heedlessness and self-blame for pride and ingratitude illustrate how a trial can turn people back.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr connects this lesson with 7:168.

view: Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh's maxim says that ingratitude exposes blessings to loss, while gratitude secures them.
Their quick regret and hope for a better replacement urge the idolaters to repent just as promptly.
Reports about the garden story say it belonged to a righteous man who left it to his people and town.
Reports variously place the garden in Yemen near Ṣanʿāʾ, in Abyssinia, or among the People of Scripture.
The garden was burned, blackened, bare, or stripped of crop and fruit, so it no longer resembled the orchard the owners knew and they failed to recognize it.
note: Al-Biqāʿī specifies that after a short walk they found no trace of crop or fruit; Ibn ʿAṭiyya places their arrival at dawn.

view: Attributing the speech to the owners in the plural indicates that they all agreed about the cause of what happened to them.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr connects the group of owners with 68:17.

view: The emphatic wording expresses grief and regret at their newly recognized earlier heedlessness.
On the lost-road reading, the following 'rather' corrects their first impression: this was indeed their own garden, destroyed and deprived of produce.
note: The correction is in the next verse.

view: At first the owners thought they had lost the road to their garden and reached the wrong place, so the ruined orchard could not be theirs.
note: This is presented as the first impression before recognition. Ṭabāṭabāʾī favors the moral reading instead.

view: After their initial mistake, the owners recognized that the ruined garden was their own.
note: Al-Nasafī says they recognized it on looking carefully; al-Ṭabarī has another brother recognize it.

view: On recognizing the garden, they understood its destruction as punishment for their wrongful plan to deny the poor.
note: Some notes state punishment without specifying the offense; others identify their exclusion of the poor or miserly resolve.

view: Their later recognition was that they had been deprived of the garden's crop, benefit, or blessing; the plan from which they expected gain had rebounded on them.
note: Ibn ʿAṭiyya includes the garden's blessing; al-Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān connect deprivation to the plan to bar the poor.

view: Alternatively, 'astray' acknowledges moral error: they had strayed from truth or right conduct by planning to harvest while withholding the poor's due, and had wrongly assumed the plan would succeed.
note: Al-Ālūsī rejects this reading; Ṭabāṭabāʾī favors it over the lost-road reading. Al-Jishumī reports both straying from truth and withholding the poor's due.

view: Their 'misguidance' can mean straying from gratitude; the metaphor shows that they understood the disaster as punishment for ingratitude.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr links this to their pride and failure to thank God.

view: They recognized that their deprivation exceeded what they had intended for the poor, leaving them despairing of both present and future.
Their deprivation followed both their denial of the poor and their omission of the exception.
Their initial mistaken belief that they had strayed, followed by recognition of earned punishment, alludes to Muhammad's opponents thinking themselves guided before realizing their error.
